text: During gangway connection between the SOV Island Clipper and the Oseberg H platform, a rupture in a hydraulic supply hose coupling caused sudden loss of hydraulic pressure. The investigation attributed the rupture to a material defect in the coupling's press sleeve that likely occurred during steel production. The gangway became inoperable and moved erratically; the cone loosened and struck the railings, triggering a facility shutdown. Disconnection attempts failed because a crossmember on the underside of the gangway became caught in the railings. Eighteen personnel were evacuated by helicopter after approximately 90 minutes. No risk assessment had considered loss of control of the gangway during disconnection, and no barrier prevented personnel access to the landing area during the operation.

On a second occasion at the same interface, a supply hose ejected from its coupling because the wrong type of coupling had been used, combined with insufficient pressure during assembly. Hydraulic pressure was lost and emergency operation of the gangway failed. Three personnel were evacuated after approximately 13 minutes. No actual injuries occurred, but the investigation concluded personal injury could not be excluded had circumstances been only slightly different.

During a lifting operation on the Symra field drilling project, a logging tool weighing 2.67 tonnes and measuring 11.81 metres was being moved from the catwalk to the pipe deck using the starboard offshore knuckle boom crane. The deck operator acting as slinger was standing in the path of the load and, at times, directly beneath it. The load was not fully under control and the logging tool swung uncontrollably during the lift, striking the deck operator in the chest area. The worker sustained a broken arm, several broken ribs, and internal injuries, and was evacuated by SAR service. The investigation found deficient expertise, inadequate lift planning, poor handover procedures at crew change, and weak safety culture.

A temporary scaffolding worker fell 4.4 metres from formwork scaffolding onto concrete flooring while assembling formwork for the emergency power generator building at Hammerfest LNG. The direct cause was that the worker lost his balance and fell; his fall-arrest harness with dual lanyard and shock absorber was not attached to a secure anchor point. The underlying cause was that the scaffolding contractor had not made provision for the use of work platforms during assembly of the formwork scaffolding. The worker sustained serious injuries; investigators noted that under slightly different circumstances he could have suffered far more serious injuries or died.

At the Njord A facility, chronic instability in the level control of the 1st-stage separator led operators to switch to manual control and leave the level control valve in a fixed position to manage the instability. The valve was left in this fixed position by mistake. This caused the water level to fall, allowing oil to mix with treated water and discharge to sea for about 2 hours 20 minutes, an estimated 75 cubic metres. The safety system's level gauge showed an incorrectly stable, higher water level than the shutdown set point, so the emergency shut-off valve on the water outlet did not close as designed. Detection occurred only when a person on the facility noticed an unusual odour; the operator toured the field, identified the source of the odour within nine minutes, and closed the water outlet manually to stop the discharge.

Fire developed in the high-voltage room of the M40 module on the unmanned Sleipner B platform. After the first of several smoke alarms went off at 04:35, the facility was shut down, depressurised, and de-energised, and a seven-person team was sent from Sleipner A to assess the situation. After an initial inspection appeared to show the situation was controlled, personnel attempted to restore power, which triggered new smoke development, prompting shutdown and withdrawal of the team. The last smoke observation was approximately 13 hours after the first detection. The most probable explanation was an electrical fault in a variable speed drive (VSD); the fire likely developed further because two fire doors into the high-voltage room were opened for ventilation and/or because voltage from Sleipner A was reapplied. No personnel were aboard at the time of ignition.

During manned underwater operations at the Goliat field, a diver made a dive to 19.5 metres lasting 75 minutes using a light diving craft and Nitrox breathing gas. The diver subsequently showed signs of cutaneous decompression sickness and possible neurological symptoms and received hyperbaric chamber treatment before being sent ashore for medical monitoring. The investigation found deficiencies in how the diving contractor accounted for uncertainty and in the application of the Norwegian Diving and Treatment Tables.

Less than two weeks after a prior decompression-sickness event on the same diving campaign, two divers developed cutaneous decompression sickness following dives exceeding 21 metres with bottom times of 86 and 88 minutes under similar conditions. No neurological symptoms were detected. Both divers received hyperbaric chamber treatment and their companion divers received preventive recompression therapy; the diving operation was subsequently terminated and demobilised. The investigation found that the operator's classification and follow-up of the first incident had been insufficient to prevent a recurrence, and that severe decompression sickness with permanent late effects could have occurred under slightly different circumstances.

During offline rigging activities on the Scarabeo 8 semi-submersible, a three-person crew was transferring a riser spider from the drill floor to the pipe deck. A transport frame carrying the spider was placed on the Riser Catwalk Machine (RCWM) but became misaligned. A floorman entered the space between the riser spider and the RCWM to unhook sling cables while the driller attempted to switch the equipment control mode from RCWM to the Drill Floor Manipulator Arm (DFMA). The mode transition failed to complete; when the driller then moved the joystick intending to move the DFMA, the RCWM instead activated and moved inward toward the worker, who had not left the red zone. The winch operator radioed an alert and the driller quickly reversed the machine, but not before the worker sustained crush injuries to both thighs. The investigation cited failure to follow red-zone procedures and control-interface confusion between RCWM and DFMA modes; it assessed that the incident could have resulted in amputation of both legs, permanent disability, or death.

A fire started in a cooling unit (DX unit) in a local equipment room within the Gina Krog living quarters. Smoke spread into the corridor, the central control room (CCR), and the emergency preparedness room because the CCR and the local equipment room were not separated by a smoke-proof and gas-tight fire division. Two probable ignition sources were identified: loose screw-clamp terminals on a circuit breaker that could cause overheating, and series resonance producing stationary voltages of more than 400V across a motor capacitor. Consequences included material damage to the DX unit, a production stoppage, and minor respiratory symptoms among CCR staff and responders; the investigation classified the missing fire division as a Class A non-conformity.

During Storm Ingunn on 31 January 2024, a large 'green water' wave washed over the deck of the Asgard A facility and struck a cabin window with force exceeding the window's load resistance, forcing the window and frame into the cabin and flooding the living quarters. No one was in the cabin at the time. The investigation found that no green-water model testing had been conducted for that window location, that the facility was not compliant with internal requirements for window coverings, and concluded that had anyone been present, the window, frame, and inrushing seawater could have caused a serious injury or fatality.

During permanent plugging and abandonment of well Q-21 on the Troll field, personnel cut the 13 3/8-inch casing at 510 metres depth. Shortly after the cut, large amounts of water and gas gushed uncontrollably onto the Deepsea Bollsta facility; approximately 930 kilograms of gas (methane, ethane, and propane) was released, and one person in the shaker room sustained a minor injury among 114 personnel aboard. The direct cause was that gas which had accumulated behind the casing was released when the casing was cut, because the outer well barrier had failed. Faulty calibration led to misinterpretation of log data, which contributed to the failure to detect the presence of gas behind casing before the cut. The investigation identified major-accident potential: under different circumstances, ignition of the released gas could have caused serious injury, fatalities, and facility damage.

event_label: Excerpt 1 of 3: initial conditions and off-gassing
text: On the morning of January 29, 2020, a workover crew arrived at the Daniel H. Wendland 1-H well in Burleson County, Texas. The recorded shut-in pressure that morning was 50 psig, down from 80 psig on each of the two previous mornings. The wellbore fluid level was approximately 4,850 feet below ground level. When the crew opened the well and bled off pressure, gas continued to evolve, rise up the wellbore, and exit from surface valves left open to the atmosphere. Workers considered this off-gassing normal for the well.

event_label: Excerpt 2 of 3: brine barrier and false 'well is dead' belief
text: To prepare for replacing the tubing head, the onsite supervisor had a contractor pump 50 barrels of 10-pound-per-gallon brine into the wellbore to establish a hydrostatic barrier for well control; no mechanical barrier was installed. The brine temporarily overbalanced the formation, but as it fell through the wellbore fluids it displaced entrained gas, which vented to atmosphere for about a minute -- a vacuum-and-venting sequence the onsite supervisor considered an expected sign that the well was 'static' or 'dead.' In fact, fluid was draining from the wellbore into the underpressured, long-completion-interval reservoir at an estimated 15 to 40 barrels per hour, so the hydrostatic barrier from the brine would have been lost to the reservoir within roughly 1.3 to 3.5 hours, well before the tubing-head work was completed.

event_label: Excerpt 3 of 3: blowout and flash fire
text: As fluid level continued to drop in the wellbore, the top of the completion interval became underbalanced and gas began flowing into the well while fluid still drained from the lower part of the interval. Workers at the location reported seeing gas venting from the open well. Workers were in the process of bolting up the wellhead when the release suddenly transitioned to a large volume of oil and gas. The hydrocarbons found an ignition source within seconds and a flash fire erupted, fatally injuring three contract workers and seriously injuring a fourth; the fire also destroyed the workover rig and several nearby vehicles.

On the evening of October 26, 2019, a plunger inside one of three positive-displacement pumps at the Aghorn Operating waterflood station failed, releasing produced water containing hydrogen sulfide (H2S) inside the pump house. At 6:38 p.m. the control board registered a high oil level alarm, and five minutes later an automatic phone notification was sent to an Aghorn employee. As part of his normal duties, the employee drove to the facility alone to investigate. After entering the pump house, he was overcome by hydrogen sulfide gas.

event_label: Excerpt 2 of 2: family exposure and detection-system failure
text: Around 9:30 p.m., having not heard from her husband for several hours, the employee's wife drove to the waterflood station with their two children (ages 6 and 9) to check on him. She appears to have entered the pump house looking for him and was also overcome by hydrogen sulfide gas. Emergency responders later rescued the two children from the car and, after donning self-contained breathing apparatus, found the bodies of both the employee and his wife inside the pump house; produced water containing H2S continued to leak from the pump for hours. The station's hydrogen sulfide detection system, comprising eight detectors including two inside the pump house, was designed to trigger a warning light atop the building automatically; post-incident testing indicated the system may not have been performing as expected, and neither responders nor Aghorn employees saw the warning light illuminated that night.

While tripping the drill string into the primary well, two floormen were positioned in the fingerboard area to spot and open fingers manually. The rig's pipe handling equipment (PHE) was being used to transfer stands from the fingerboard area to well centre. The injured party, a floorman, was positioned at the upper derrick level tying a finger latch open when the PHE moved toward its next targeted finger slot while he was still on the fingers. The PHE arm extended and pinned the floorman's left upper arm; he called an immediate 'all stop' and the assistant driller retracted the PHE, releasing his arm. A similar incident had occurred previously. Contributing factors included that the finger latch area was not clearly defined and understood as a red-zone area during tubular movement, and that safety-critical communication standards were not established and maintained.

Two personnel were performing loose lifting-gear inspections around the riser deck of an offshore drilling unit, visually inspecting slings and recording serial numbers. Five metal deck-strengthening plates were stacked vertically on dunnage and secured to a stanchion by a single 2-inch ratchet strap, with slings still rigged from a prior crane lift left in place for convenience. The inspection team leader freed one sling but found a second sling pinched between the plates and the stanchion; he asked his assistant to loosen the ratchet strap to free it, then leaned his back against the plates, apparently to hold them in position. When the ratchet strap was released, the hook let go and the plates fell forward under their own weight, fatally trapping the team leader between the plates and the drilling bail-rack framework. The task had drifted from a low-risk visual inspection into removing rigged slings from sea-fastened cargo without the team recognising the change in risk profile.

A crewman was changing rubber stops on the forward Pipe Racking System (PRS) track at the 144-foot level of the derrick. He was wearing a safety harness with his lanyard tied off to the PRS track. During this task, the driller moved the PRS along the track at the request of the PRS programmer, which moved the unit out from underneath the man working aloft. He felt the movement and arrested his fall by grabbing his lanyard, then lowered himself and hung suspended from the track until the driller was alerted and stopped the movement; he was lowered to the floor in a personnel workbasket with no injuries. The investigation found that two maintenance tasks were being carried out simultaneously without adequate communication between the serviceman, driller, and crewman aloft, and that lock-out/tag-out procedures were not in use.

While running the 60th joint of 13 3/8-inch casing using a casing running tool, the single-joint casing elevators (SJE) were not latched and pinned correctly. With the winch line and sling removed from the joint, the driller was signaled to pick up the casing; when weight was taken up, the elevators opened and the joint fell out of the V-door, continued down the catwalk, and came to rest against the wireline unit, causing slight equipment damage but with potential for a fatality. Post-incident inspection found the elevators had not failed mechanically: they were only partially latched, leaving enough room to insert the retaining safety pin behind the latching device instead of in front of it, so the pin did not perform its retaining function. The worker latching the elevators did not know they were not fully latched, the driller's view of the V-door was obstructed by stacked drill pipe and had to rely on a hand signal, and no second person was assigned to check that the elevators were latched and pinned correctly.

Rig crews had just finished positioning a rack of nitrogen cylinders to begin pre-charging accumulator cylinders. One nitrogen cylinder, charged to 2,400 psi and part of a rack not itself connected to the charging process, ruptured at its base, scattering the rack, debris, and the remaining 11 cylinders across the immediate area and the port aft area of the rig. Three employees suffered minor first-aid injuries and were evacuated and later released to return to work; the calculated fatal blast zone for a cylinder of this size at 2,400 psi is approximately 1.5 metres. Rig operations were stopped and a safety stand-down held while all remaining nitrogen cylinders were bled down to atmospheric pressure. Investigators found the ruptured cylinder's base was heavily corroded, other cylinders in the same rack showed similar but less severe corrosion, and visual pre-fill inspections before mobilisation had not included disassembling the rack to inspect the cylinder bases, where the corrosion was located.

While a drilling unit was working in the North Sea in weather of 60-knot winds and a 5.0-metre sea state, a lifeboat unexpectedly descended from its normally stowed position to the sea without human intervention, due to a winch failure. As the lifeboat reached the sea, the crew went to the winch location and tried to arrest further cable deployment, but the stern wire failed in the weather conditions, leaving the lifeboat held only by the bow wire; the bow wire later parted and the lifeboat drifted away before being recovered. Investigation found the winch's gas strut had corroded until the piston rod's compromised surface allowed pressurised gas to escape, that the strut material was not suited to the marine environment, that maintenance guidance lacked clear inspection/replacement intervals for the component, and that the system relied on the single gas strut with no redundancy.

While the deck crew was engaged in heli-deck operations, a third-party inspector disembarked and received an onboarding induction before being shown to the pipe deck, where completion tools awaited function testing. Minutes later the deck crew returned and resumed transferring 7-inch joints of casing from the pipe deck to the catwalk machine using a knuckle-boom crane (KBC) and gripper yoke. As the banksman positioned the gripper yoke over the fourth joint, the third-party inspector shouted to him; the banksman radioed the KBC operator and walked toward the inspector, placing a foot between two casing joints as he did so. The KBC operator closed the gripper yoke, which was misaligned over the target joint, and it struck the banksman, causing several bone fractures. The investigation found the banksman had not known the inspector was working within the barrier, was not positioned to see the lifting team, and that radio instructions were not confirmed between banksman and operator; a toolbox talk had not been held before recommencing the activity, the task risk assessment and lift plan in use were generic rather than activity-specific, and the activity had not been recognised as a blind lift requiring a permit.

During a tripping operation for cementing pipe, crew members discovered a 25.4 cm (10 inch) diameter, 0.68 kg (1.5 lb) brass thrust washer on the rig floor, which had detached from the crown assembly top sheave and narrowly missed a worker by approximately 2 metres. Investigation found the sheave pin had shifted laterally, causing the sheave to lean from its proper vertical position, and that the outer sheave locking plate bolts had sheared, with the plate itself resting on the edge of the crown assembly. No injuries were reported. Rig operations were suspended until repairs were completed.
